entries.summary: Government Identifier stored as an ordinary character field.
entries.rationale: KYCDocument keeps the document number in a plain CharField beside a document_type whose choices include Aadhaar and PAN. Neither the field nor the model defines field-level encryption, tokenisation or a custom field class, so the Government Identifier is written to the PostgreSQL column as received. Compose adds no encrypted volume or database encryption setting that would lower the severity.
entries.personal_data: Government Identifier (document number: Aadhaar, PAN, passport, driving licence)

entries.summary: Identity document and selfie images stored without field-level protection.
entries.rationale: The document, front, back and selfie images are plain ImageFields uploaded to kyc_documents/ and kyc_selfies/ under MEDIA_ROOT (backend/kyc_platform/settings.py:143). The files carry Government Identifiers and facial images (Biometric) and no encryption, tokenisation or access-restricted storage class is applied before they are written.
entries.personal_data: Identity document images (Government Identifier) and selfie images (Biometric)

entries.summary: OCR text and structured extraction output stored in plain columns.
entries.rationale: extracted_text (TextField) and extracted_data (JSONField) receive the OCR output. The OCR service builds structured data containing aadhaar_number, pan_number, passport_number and date_of_birth (ai-services/services/ocr_service.py:126-145, 182, 200), so these columns can hold Government Identifiers and dates of birth; no field-level encryption or tokenisation is defined for them.
entries.personal_data: Government Identifier (Aadhaar, PAN, passport numbers), name, date of birth in OCR output

entries.summary: Contact and profile fields of the account model are plain columns; their tier is not settled by code.
entries.rationale: email, phone_number, date_of_birth and address are ordinary model fields with no field-level protection. The code settles that they are unprotected, but the Issue Type applies to Tier A/B Personal Data Elements and the code carries no tier assignment for Contact or Profile elements.
entries.personal_data: Contact (email, phone number, address) and date of birth
entries.reason: Whether these Contact/Profile Elements fall in Tier A/B is a classification outside the code. A documented Data Category-to-tier assignment for Contact and date of birth would settle it.

entries.summary: VerificationAttempt.ocr_result is a plain JSON column intended for OCR service output.
entries.rationale: ocr_result is declared as an ordinary JSONField beneath the comment 'AI Service results'. If it stores the OCR response it would hold the identifiers named above, but no code in the repository writes this model.
entries.personal_data: Possibly Government Identifier and name from the OCR response
entries.reason: No code populates VerificationAttempt, so its contents are unknown. A writer that saves the raw OCR response into ocr_result would settle it.

entries.summary: GovernmentVerification request and response payloads stored in plain JSON columns.
entries.rationale: request_data and response_data are ordinary JSONFields on the model that records results from Government API checks. A verification request would plausibly carry the document number, but nothing in the repository builds or stores these payloads.
entries.personal_data: Possibly Government Identifier sent to and returned by Government APIs
entries.reason: No code creates GovernmentVerification rows, so the payload contents are unknown. The code that builds request_data would settle it.

entries.summary: Aadhaar numbers can be stored in a plain database column.
entries.rationale: DocumentType includes AADHAAR (line 11) and the document_number field that follows document_type is an ordinary CharField with no vault, reference token or masking indirection. An Aadhaar number extracted by OCR is therefore stored as the Government Identifier itself in the application database.
entries.personal_data: Aadhaar number

entries.summary: OCR response returns the Aadhaar number unmasked.
entries.rationale: The OCR route returns the full extracted text and structured_data to its caller. The OCR service sets data['aadhaar_number'] to the full 12-digit match with spaces removed (ocr_service.py:179-182), and nothing in the route masks it before it is returned.
entries.personal_data: Aadhaar number

entries.summary: Results page displays the document number without masking.
entries.rationale: The results page renders extractedData.documentNumber verbatim in a monospace span with no masking to the last four digits. The VerificationResult type (frontend/src/services/api.ts) names this field as the document number, and the AI service returns a full 12-digit Aadhaar number for Aadhaar documents (ai-services/services/ocr_service.py:179-182), so an Aadhaar number would be displayed in full. The code that fills the field is inconsistent (api.ts reads document_number from the OCR extracted_text, which is a string), so which values reach it at runtime is not shown; the unmasked rendering is the code fact.
entries.personal_data: Aadhaar number (and other document numbers)

entries.summary: Django SECRET_KEY has a committed fallback value.
entries.rationale: SECRET_KEY is read from the environment but falls back to a literal 'django-insecure-' value committed in source (value masked here). Docker Compose does not set SECRET_KEY, so a default deployment signs sessions, CSRF tokens and any JWT (SIMPLE_JWT, settings.py:170-175) with the committed key. The Issue Type needs the key to protect named Personal Data Elements, and the code does not show that: every view sets AllowAny (backend/kyc/views.py:19, 77), no model is registered in any admin.py, and IsAuthenticated (settings.py:155) is the default for views that do not exist, so no route serving document numbers or OCR data (backend/kyc/models.py:30,37-38) sits behind a session or token signed with this key.
entries.personal_data: Government Identifier and OCR data in KYC records protected by the signed sessions and tokens
entries.reason: No route or admin model that serves KYC records is protected by sessions or JWTs signed with SECRET_KEY: all views are AllowAny and the admin registers no model. A view or admin model that returns KYC records behind session or JWT authentication would settle it.

entries.summary: PostgreSQL credentials are committed in Compose.
entries.rationale: The Compose postgres service sets POSTGRES_PASSWORD to a literal and the same literal is repeated inside DATABASE_URL for the backend, AI service, worker and beat services (lines 35, 53, 70, 88; value masked). The database stores document numbers and OCR data (backend/kyc/models.py:30-38), so the hard-coded credential protects named Personal Data Elements.
entries.personal_data: Government Identifier and OCR data stored in PostgreSQL

entries.summary: Django DEBUG defaults to True and Compose sets DEBUG=1.
entries.rationale: DEBUG falls back to True when the environment is silent and docker-compose.yml sets DEBUG=1 for the backend, worker and beat. With DEBUG true Django serves detailed error pages that include settings and local variables. The backend handles document numbers and OCR text (backend/kyc/serializers.py:11-16), but the code does not show an error path that places those values in a response.
entries.personal_data: Possibly Government Identifier and OCR text, if an error page captures them
entries.reason: Whether an error response actually contains a Personal Data Element depends on runtime failures and on the deployed DEBUG value. A captured error response carrying a document number, or a production environment file, would settle it.

entries.summary: AI service returns raw exception text in 500 responses.
entries.rationale: The forgery, face-match, liveness and complete-verification routes put str(e) into the HTTP 500 detail (lines 189, 225, 256, 287), and the error JSON also returns the full request URL. Exception text from image decoding is not shown to include Personal Data, and the OCR route uses a fixed message instead.
evidence: ai-services/main.py:189: raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=f"Forgery detection failed: {str(e)}")
entries.personal_data: Possibly identity or selfie image content, if an exception message echoes it
entries.reason: Static code does not show that an exception message contains a Personal Data Element. An error response, or a library error that echoes input bytes, would settle it.

entries.summary: Unauthenticated history route returns every KYC record.
entries.rationale: KYCVerificationView sets permission_classes = [AllowAny] (line 19) overriding the IsAuthenticated default, and GET serialises KYCDocument.objects.all() with no filter on the requesting Data Principal. The serializer includes document_number, extracted_text and extracted_data (serializers.py:14-16), so any caller reads every Data Principal's Government Identifier and OCR data. The results page calls this route and is written to show the first record of the global list (frontend/src/app/kyc/results/page.tsx:32-34); whether it renders at runtime is not needed, because the route itself returns every record to any caller.
entries.personal_data: Government Identifier (document number: Aadhaar, PAN, passport, driving licence), OCR text, name and date of birth of all Data Principals

entries.summary: OCR route processes identity documents without authentication.
entries.rationale: POST /ocr/extract has no authentication dependency and returns Government Identifiers extracted from the supplied image (lines 139-151). It returns only data derived from the caller's own upload and stores nothing, so no other Data Principal's record is exposed by the code shown. Compose publishes the service on port 8001 (docker-compose.yml:50-51).
entries.personal_data: Government Identifier extracted from the uploaded document
entries.reason: The route does not read stored records, so a missing ownership check is not shown. Deployment topology showing whether port 8001 is reachable by untrusted callers, or a caller-supplied identifier selecting stored data, would settle it.

entries.summary: History serializer exposes full document number and raw OCR data.
entries.rationale: The serializer lists explicit fields including the unmasked document_number, the raw extracted_text and the whole extracted_data JSON; it does not use '__all__' and omits images and the user relation. Whether serialising these fields meets this Issue Type's 'whole model or nested records' boundary depends on its definition, and the unauthenticated exposure of the same fields is recorded under SEC-07.
entries.personal_data: Government Identifier (document number: Aadhaar, PAN, passport, driving licence), OCR text and structured extraction output
entries.reason: The serializer is an explicit field list, not a whole-model dump. A ruling that raw OCR text and the extracted_data JSON count as nested records, or a runtime response showing unrelated fields, would settle it.

entries.summary: AI service allows any origin with credentials.
entries.rationale: CORSMiddleware is configured with allow_origins ['*'], allow_credentials True and wildcard methods and headers. The service accepts identity document and selfie images and returns unmasked OCR text and identifiers (lines 113-151, 192-225), so the permissive policy sits on routes handling Government Identifiers and facial images.
evidence: ai-services/main.py:38: allow_origins=["*"],  # Configure appropriately for production
entries.personal_data: Government Identifier and facial images handled by the AI service routes

entries.summary: Document and selfie uploads default to plain HTTP.
entries.rationale: uploadFile posts the identity document or selfie to AI_SERVICES_URL, whose default is http://localhost:8001 (line 4) and which Compose also sets to http://localhost:8001 (docker-compose.yml:107). No https scheme or redirect is configured anywhere, so the images travel without transport encryption. The URL is a localhost default that the deployer overrides through NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables, and Compose sets it to the loopback host, so loopback traffic is not shown to cross a network in plaintext; whether any real deployment uses an http:// address depends on a value outside the code.
entries.personal_data: Identity document images (Government Identifier) and selfie images (Biometric)
entries.reason: The scheme and host come from NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_AI_SERVICES_URL, which default to loopback http://localhost addresses. A deployment config or environment file that sets a non-loopback http:// address (or a reverse proxy config terminating plain HTTP) would settle it.

entries.summary: Face-match upload sends both images over plain HTTP.
entries.rationale: matchFaces posts document_image and selfie_image to AI_SERVICES_URL, which defaults to and is configured as an http:// URL (api.ts:4; docker-compose.yml:107). Both the identity document and the facial image are sent without transport encryption. The URL is a localhost default that the deployer overrides through NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables, and Compose sets it to the loopback host, so loopback traffic is not shown to cross a network in plaintext; whether any real deployment uses an http:// address depends on a value outside the code.
entries.personal_data: Identity document image (Government Identifier) and selfie image (Biometric)
entries.reason: The scheme and host come from NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_AI_SERVICES_URL, which default to loopback http://localhost addresses. A deployment config or environment file that sets a non-loopback http:// address (or a reverse proxy config terminating plain HTTP) would settle it.

entries.summary: Verification result with extracted identity data is posted over plain HTTP.
entries.rationale: saveVerificationResult posts the VerificationResult, whose extractedData holds name, document number, date of birth and nationality, to API_BASE_URL, defaulting to http://localhost:8000 (line 3; docker-compose.yml:106). No https scheme is enforced. The URL is a localhost default that the deployer overrides through NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables, and Compose sets it to the loopback host, so loopback traffic is not shown to cross a network in plaintext; whether any real deployment uses an http:// address depends on a value outside the code.
entries.personal_data: Name, document number (Government Identifier), date of birth, nationality
entries.reason: The scheme and host come from NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_AI_SERVICES_URL, which default to loopback http://localhost addresses. A deployment config or environment file that sets a non-loopback http:// address (or a reverse proxy config terminating plain HTTP) would settle it.

entries.summary: Persistent PostgreSQL volume has no configured backup.
entries.rationale: Compose deploys PostgreSQL with a persistent postgres_data volume that holds KYC document numbers and OCR data (backend/kyc/models.py:30-38). No backup service, scheduled dump, replica or backup setting appears in Compose or any other config; RUN_COMMANDS.md:200-206 only documents a manual pg_dump, which is not a configured backup. Uploaded images sit under backend/media on a bind mount with no backup either.
entries.personal_data: Government Identifier, OCR data and identity images persisted in the store

entries.summary: PostgreSQL port is published on the host.
entries.rationale: The postgres service maps 5432:5432 with no host address restriction, and the database holds Government Identifiers and OCR data (backend/kyc/models.py:30-38) behind a credential committed in the same file (line 10). Whether the port is reachable from outside depends on the host firewall, but the Compose configuration itself publishes it.
entries.personal_data: Government Identifier and OCR data in the database

entries.summary: Backend container runs as root with the Django development server.
entries.rationale: The backend image is built FROM python:3.11-slim (line 1), declares no USER, and starts python manage.py runserver. The container therefore runs as root while serving routes that read and write Government Identifiers and identity images.

entries.summary: AI service container runs as root with auto-reload.
entries.rationale: The AI service image is built FROM python:3.11-slim (line 1), declares no USER, and starts uvicorn with --reload. The container runs as root while processing identity document and selfie images.
entries.personal_data: Identity document and selfie images processed by the AI service

entries.summary: Verification starts with no consent step or notice.
entries.rationale: startVerification checks only that two files are present, then uploads the identity document and selfie to the OCR, forgery, face and liveness routes and posts the result to the backend (lines 113, 154, 195, 236, 305). No consent control, notice or server-side consent check precedes processing. The Applicability Assumption treats processing as consent-based unless the code shows a legitimate use, and an upload the Data Principal starts voluntarily for verification may fall under §7.
evidence: frontend/src/app/kyc/start/page.tsx:63: showError('Please upload both a document and a selfie photo to continue.', 'warning');
entries.personal_data: Identity document image (Government Identifier) and selfie image (Biometric)
entries.reason: Whether this processing is covered by a §7 legitimate use (voluntary provision, or a legal obligation behind KYC) is not stated in code; README.md says only that the platform supports banking compliance. A statement of the Data Fiduciary's lawful basis would settle it.

entries.summary: Backend creates KYC records with no consent check.
entries.rationale: The POST handler validates and saves the serializer with no Consent Record lookup or Enforcement Point, and permission_classes is AllowAny. Whether this is a gap depends on the same lawful-basis question as the front end.
entries.personal_data: Document number (Government Identifier) and OCR data saved to the database
entries.reason: Whether a §7 legitimate use covers the saved record is not settled by code. A stated lawful basis would settle it.

entries.summary: Onboarding collects date of birth with no age gate or parental consent.
entries.rationale: The account model has a date_of_birth field and the OCR service extracts date_of_birth from documents, so the application collects age data. The onboarding flow begins processing as soon as two files are uploaded; no age check, date-of-birth comparison or parental-consent step exists in the frontend, backend views, serializers or AI service.

entries.summary: Verification ends with a stated 12-month validity and no erasure of the stored records.
entries.rationale: The results page tells an approved Data Principal that the verification is valid for 12 months and tells a rejected one that it could not be completed, which marks an end of purpose in code. Nothing deletes or expires the KYCDocument rows, images or OCR data afterwards: no delete route, scheduled task, retention setting or erasure job exists, and compliance/models.py:102 defines expires_at on RiskAssessment that nothing reads.

entries.summary: Exception text from the save of a KYC record is written to the log and may carry the failing row.
entries.rationale: KYCVerificationView.post saves a KYCDocument that holds document_number and extracted_text, and its catch-all handler writes the exception text to the logger with an f-string (views.py:48-49); the root logger routes to console and logs/django.log (settings.py:219-222). The serializer omits the required user foreign key (serializers.py:11-27; models.py:28 has no null=True), so a payload with a valid document_type and document_number reaches an INSERT that fails the NOT NULL constraint. PostgreSQL, the database Compose deploys, puts the failing row's values in the error DETAIL, which is part of str(e), so the logged text can contain the document number and OCR data. Static code does not show the driver's message.
evidence: backend/kyc/views.py:49: logger.error(f"Unexpected error in KYC verification: {e}")
entries.personal_data: Possibly Government Identifier (document number) and OCR text in the failing row
entries.reason: Whether the logged exception text contains a Personal Data Element depends on the database driver's error message. A captured log line from a failed POST to /api/kyc/verifications/ showing the failing row would settle it.
